summary: Field Shift is a prototype that turns NASA data into planting and crop-rotation advice for farmers, in Palestinian Arabic. It started with an interview with a farmer in Saffa, near Ramallah. He grows cauliflower with little irrigation water and usually plants in early September. Our rule-based model uses ten seasons of historical data from NASA POWER: MERRA-2 temperature, humidity and wind, CERES solar radiation, and GPM IMERG rainfall. For each planting date and crop rotation, it estimates heat stress on seedlings and irrigation needs (FAO-56 Penman–Monteith). It then ranks the options against an assumed water budget. For Saffa, planting on 11–20 October instead of 1 September cuts hot days in the first three weeks from about 16 to 3. Estimated irrigation falls from about 262 to 98 m³ per dunum. The model suggests rainfed faba bean as the next crop. The farmer asks by voice or text in a WhatsApp-style chat and gets the answer and the reason in Arabic. The figures are model estimates. A field trial on two strips of his land is planned to test them.
details:
WHAT WE BUILT
Field Shift is a prototype that helps a farmer make two decisions every season: when to plant, and what to grow next. It answers in Palestinian Arabic, by text or voice, in a WhatsApp-style chat.

THE FARMER BEHIND IT
We interviewed a farmer in Saffa, a village west of Ramallah. He grows cauliflower, cabbage and broccoli with limited irrigation water and usually plants in early September. He avoids July and August because of heat, water shortage and disease. NASA data shows the problem: after a 1 September planting, about 16 of the first 21 days are above 32 °C (historical average over ten seasons).

HOW IT WORKS
1. The farmer asks in his own words, for example: «بدي أزرع زهرة والمي عندي قليلة. إمتى أزرع وشو أزرع بعدها؟» ("I want to plant cauliflower and I have little water. When should I plant, and what next?").
2. A rule-based model compares seven planting dates (1 September to 31 October, every 10 days) and three crop rotations over ten historical seasons. For each option it estimates:
- heat stress on young seedlings (days above 32 °C in the first 21 days),
- irrigation need: FAO-56 Penman–Monteith crop water demand minus effective rainfall,
- soil and rotation effects (legumes earn a credit; brassicas in two winters running are penalised),
- fit with the farmer's usual practice.
Options are scored against the farmer's water budget (100 m³ per dunum per season in our scenario).
3. The farmer gets one short Arabic reply with icons and can tap

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"▶" ]

to hear it. Asking «ليش؟» ("why?") explains the reason.

RESULT FOR SAFFA (model estimates)
Planting on 11–20 October instead of 1 September cuts hot days in the first three weeks from about 16 to 3, and estimated irrigation for the cauliflower season from about 262 to 98 m³ per dunum. For the next winter, rainfed faba bean ranked above cabbage (score 85 vs 77): about 98 vs 226 m³ per dunum over both seasons, and the legume breaks the run of brassica crops.

WHY IT MATTERS
Water is the main limit for small farmers around Ramallah. A planting shift costs nothing to try and can save water and seedlings. Field Shift turns global NASA data into a decision one farmer can act on, in his own language, without reading charts.

HOW WE TESTED IT
We tuned the model on 2001/02–2014/15, froze it, and ran it on 2015/16–2024/25. The top recommendation stays the same with either NASA rainfall source. 27 of 28 pipeline checks pass (a geographic holdout was not possible with one data cell). Automated tests cover the model, the Arabic chat and the voice flow. The chat answers only agriculture questions.

LIMITS AND NEXT STEP
All figures are model estimates for one NASA weather cell, which several villages share. Our next step is a field trial with the farmer: one strip planted in early September and one in mid-October, measuring irrigation used and seedling losses.

TOOLS
Python (model, data checks, web server), HTML/JavaScript (chat page), browser speech recognition and speech synthesis for Arabic voice, and NASA POWER, GPM IMERG and SRTM data.
